summary: A Live Science roundup of photos and reactions from a strong G3 geomagnetic storm on Nov. 5, 2023, which produced auroras as far south as Greece and Turkey. The storm was driven by two coronal mass ejections, and the article explains how such storms create auroras. It also features the aurora-like phenomenon STEVE, with photos and quotes from skywatchers in the UK, Ireland, Montana and Australia.
one_line: Photos and accounts of auroras and STEVE seen worldwide during the G3 geomagnetic storm of Nov. 5, 2023, driven by two CMEs.
key_facts: The geomagnetic storm peaked as a strong G3 on Nov. 5, 2023 at 12:40 p.m. EST (1740 GMT) on NOAA's 5-grade scale.
Northern lights were reported as far south as Greece and Turkey.
According to spaceweather.com, two coronal mass ejections hit Earth on Nov. 4 and Nov. 5 and triggered the storm.
During a solar storm, energized particles hit Earth's atmosphere at speeds up to 45 million mph (72 million km/h), and Earth's magnetic field funnels them toward the poles.
Debby Thorne photographed a vibrant pink aurora from Cullen on the Moray Firth in Scotland with an iPhone 14 Pro in night mode on Nov. 5.
Meteorologist Angel Enriquez photographed pink and green aurora over a round observatory in Glasgow, Montana, after a coworker texted 'GO OUTSIDE NOW'.
Josh Dury captured red auroral pillars low on the north horizon from the Mendip Hills in Somerset, UK.
Alistair Hamill photographed his first sub-auroral arc of solar cycle 25 at Glenarm.
STEVE stands for Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement and is a distinct phenomenon from aurora, per the American Geophysical Union.
STEVE is caused by hot (5,400 °F or 3000 °C) streams of gas snaking through Earth's magnetosphere that emit light when energized by geomagnetic storms.
Steven lomas photographed STEVE above Dunstanburgh Castle, Northumberland, UK, calling it the strongest aurora display in 8 years of photography.
Martin McKenna, observing aurora since 1998 with 180 displays, saw STEVE for the first time over Swatragh, extending across the sky and flaring near Jupiter.
Paul Pichugin captured a timelapse of the aurora australis over Busselton, Western Australia.
